lis-c-vorony.s: On Lisbon’s coat of arms there is a boat, and on it two black birds: ravens. An old legend says that ravens guarded the body of Saint Vincent on the ship that sailed to the shore of Lisbon. The boat with the ravens became the symbol of the city. You can see it on lamp posts, on flags and on houses in the city. You just have to look carefully around you.

lis-c-metro-chajka.s: Lisbon’s metro lines have lovely names. The blue line is called “Gaivota”, which means “seagull”. The yellow one is “Girassol”, “sunflower”. And the green one is “Caravela”, like an old sailing ship. These symbols are still drawn on the signs. In many stations the walls are decorated with paintings by artists, so you can ride along as if through an exhibition.

lis-c-obrigado.s: Portuguese people say “thank you” in different ways. A man or a boy says “obrigado”, and a woman or a girl says “obrigada”. The word means “I am grateful to you”, and it changes depending on who is speaking. For grown-up tourists this is a surprise: you have to remember who you are. Shop assistants in Lisbon cafés smile when they hear the right word.

lis-c-belyo.s: You walk through an old part of Lisbon and see washing drying on lines from the windows. Shirts, towels and socks flutter like flags. The streets here are narrow, and the lines are stretched right across them. There is lots of sun in the city, and the wind from the ocean dries everything quickly. For tourists it is a funny picture, and for the people who live there it is just ordinary life.

lis-c-bloshinyj-rynok.s: Twice a week, on Tuesdays and Saturdays, Lisbon has a flea market called Feira da Ladra. They sell old things here: cups, coins, books, clocks, tiles and toys. You can bargain and hunt for treasure. The name means “the thief’s fair”, but don’t be scared: the sellers here are kind, and the things are waiting for new owners.

lis-c-probka.s: In Lisbon’s shops they sell bags, purses and postcards made of cork. It is made from the bark of the cork oak. The bark is carefully taken off, like a little coat, and then the tree keeps on growing. After about nine years, the bark can be taken off again. Cork is light and soft, and it hardly gets wet. That is why it is even used to make mats for hot cups.

lis-c-lica-na-stene.s: In Lisbon there are lots of street paintings on the houses. One famous artist, called Vhils, makes portraits in an unusual way: he doesn’t paint, he chips the picture out of the wall, taking away layers of plaster and paint. The result is big faces, as if carved from stone. You walk down the street and suddenly your eyes meet those of a huge person.
a: He chips them out of the wall
He draws them in pencil on paper
He models them out of clay

lis-c-rynok-obed.s: Lisbon has an old covered market called Mercado da Ribeira. From early morning they sell vegetables, fruit, fish and flowers. And inside there is also a big hall with lots of little kitchens. You stand in a queue, take some soup, fish or a sweet treat, and sit down at a long shared table. Strangers sit next to you, but everyone here is friendly.
a: Have lunch at a shared table

lis-c-bola-na-plyazhe.s: In summer, on the beaches near Lisbon, you can hear a shout: “Bola de Berlim!” That is the name of a fluffy round bun that is fried and sprinkled with sugar. Sweet egg cream goes inside. The seller walks over the hot sand with a big basket and calls to everyone who is hungry after a swim. Eat it carefully, so the cream doesn’t run down your fingers.

lis-a-lift-santa-zhushta.s: Lisbon has a real lift in the middle of a street. It is a tall tower of dark iron with patterns like lace. It is 45 metres high, and the lift opened in 1902. It is called Santa Justa. Inside there are wooden cabins, and they carry people from the lower town, Baixa, up to the upper area, Chiado. Walking would mean climbing a steep hill! And from the platform at the top you can see red roofs, the castle and the wide river.
a: The two banks of the river

lis-a-krasnyj-most.s: A huge red bridge spans the River Tagus. It is called the 25 de Abril Bridge. It is long: more than two kilometres. Cars drive along the top, and trains run below them, one floor down. Do you know what it looks like? The famous Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco in America! The bridge is the same orange-red colour, and an American company built it. When it is foggy in Lisbon, the bridge’s towers disappear in the white mist.

lis-a-most-vasko-da-gama.s: Lisbon has another bridge too: the Vasco da Gama Bridge. It opened in 1998. With its approach roads, it stretches for about seventeen kilometres, and it is one of the longest bridges in Europe! The bridge crosses the widest part of the River Tagus, where the water looks like the sea. When you ride across it, it feels as if there are no banks at all: just water, sky and white pillars. And nearby, birds rest on the water.

lis-a-pavliny-na-zamke.s: On the hill above Alfama stands St George’s Castle. It has thick stone walls and eleven towers. But the main residents of the castle are the peacocks! They stroll around the courtyard, stretch their necks proudly and sometimes open their huge fan tails. And from the castle you can see the whole city: roofs, the river and the bridges. Children love to climb on the wall and look for their own home from above. It is one of the best lookout places in Lisbon.

lis-a-alfama-uzkie-ulochki.s: Alfama is one of the oldest parts of Lisbon. The little streets here are so narrow that two grown-ups can hardly pass each other! They wind up and down, dive under arches and end in little flights of steps. Between the houses, washing dries on lines, flowers stand on the windowsills and cats sit in the windows. From open doors comes the smell of fried fish. It is easy to get lost in Alfama, but it isn’t scary at all: in the end, all the roads lead down to the river anyway.

lis-a-bajsha-pryamye-ulicy.s: Baixa is the area at the very bottom, between the hills. Its streets are straight and even, like the squares in an exercise book. That is how the minister, the Marquis of Pombal, planned it when the city was built again: he wanted it to be roomy and easy to understand. The streets are named Rua Áurea (Golden Street), Rua da Prata (Silver Street) and Rua Augusta. Long ago, goldsmiths and silversmiths worked on them. The name “Baixa” means “low”. It is easy to walk here and not get lost.
a: Straight, like squares in an exercise book

lis-a-pessoa-za-stolikom.s: In the Chiado area, at the door of the old café A Brasileira, there is a bronze man in a hat and glasses. He sits at a little table as if he had just come out for a coffee. This is the poet Fernando Pessoa. He lived in Lisbon, loved his city and wrote poems. Tourists sit down next to him, put an arm round his shoulder and have their photo taken. You can sit next to him too, but don’t disturb him while he is thinking about poems.
a: A bronze man at a table
A stone rider on a horse
An ice statue on a roof

lis-a-funikuler-bika.s: Lisbon has a street so steep that even riding up it is hard. For it, they thought up a small yellow car: the Bica funicular. It has been running since 1892. The car is very short, like a box on rails, and the rails lie right in the middle of the road. It goes slowly, and around it are colourful houses with washing and a view of the river below. A cable pulls the funicular up, and one car goes up while the other comes down.

lis-a-funikuler-gloriya.s: Another Lisbon funicular is called Glória. It was built in 1885, and it climbs from Restauradores Square to the Bairro Alto area. The cars are yellow, and the walls along the track are covered with bright pictures and writing: artists painted them with spray cans. The ride takes about three minutes. But at the top a lovely viewpoint and a garden with trees are waiting for you. And if you are very tired, just ride it up and back down.

lis-a-ploshchad-torgovli.s: If you walk up to the River Tagus, you come to a huge square with yellow buildings around it. It is called Commerce Square (Praça do Comércio). On three sides there are long galleries with arches, and on the fourth side is the river, with steps going right down to the water. Long ago, a royal palace stood here, so the square was called “the palace yard”. In the middle stands a bronze king on a horse. Here you can run, feed the pigeons and watch the ships.

lis-a-arka-ulitsy-augusta.s: The pedestrian Rua Augusta begins at Commerce Square, and over it stands a tall stone arch. It is decorated with stone figures and a clock. Inside the arch there is a lift and a staircase, so you can go up to the top! There is a small platform there with round columns. From here you can see the streets of Baixa like straight squares, the square with its yellow walls, and the river. Below the arch, musicians play, and the sound of a guitar drifts up to you.
a: Go up and look at the city

lis-a-monastyr-zheronimush.s: In the Belém area stands the huge white Jerónimos Monastery. Building began more than five hundred years ago, at the start of the sixteenth century, when Portuguese sailors were coming back from long voyages. So the craftsmen carved on the stone not only flowers, but also ropes, shells and sailors’ knots. In the courtyard there is a long gallery with arches, as delicate as lace. It is so quiet and bright here that you can hear footsteps rustle. Try to find a sea rope or a shell among the stone patterns!

lis-a-pamyatnik-korabl.s: On the riverbank in Belém stands a white stone monument that looks like the bow of a ship. It rises up like a sail and is called the Monument to the Discoveries. In front stands Prince Henry, the one who sent ships on their way. Behind him are lined up sailors, scientists and craftsmen: more than thirty figures, and all are looking at the water. The monument is about fifty metres high, and you can go up to the very top and look at the river.

lis-a-rozovyj-dvorets.s: Next to the monastery in Belém stands a pink palace with white windows. It is called Belém Palace. Today the President of Portugal works here. A guard stands in the courtyard, and sometimes you can see an officer in a smart uniform at the entrance. Behind the palace there is a big garden with paths, flowers and old trees. Not every country paints its main buildings pink, but Portugal does it boldly! This colour is cheerful on a sunny day.

lis-a-bashnya-vasko-da-gama.s: The Parque das Nações (Park of Nations) was built on the bank of the Tagus in 1998 for a big exhibition, Expo, about the oceans. It is a new area with wide squares, fountains and gardens by the water. One of the tallest buildings here is the Vasco da Gama Tower, about 145 metres. It looks like the sail of a ship. And nearby, the long Vasco da Gama Bridge stretches across the river, and its white pillars go on to the very horizon. In the evening, lights come on along the river, and the whole waterfront glows like a party garland.

lis-a-pavilhao-conhecimento.s: In the Parque das Nações there is a museum for children and grown-ups where you can touch everything. It is called the Pavilion of Knowledge (Pavilhão do Conhecimento). Here you can turn things and press buttons, look at how everything works, and do experiments yourself. And next to it stands the Portugal Pavilion: its concrete roof hangs over the square like a huge sheet of paper held up at its two ends. It is a good place under it to hide from the sun and the rain.

lis-a-santa-luzia.s: The Santa Luzia viewpoint is a small terrace on the hill above Alfama. Over it is a wooden arbour covered in bright pink bougainvillea flowers. On the walls hang big pictures made of blue tiles, and there are benches all around. From here you can see Alfama’s red roofs, the white dome of a church, and the River Tagus with its ships. You can sit in the shade of the flowers and rest after a long climb.

lis-a-gras-pod-sosnami.s: On one of the highest hills, near the Graça area, there is a viewpoint under tall pine trees. There is shade, it is quiet and it smells lovely of pine needles. There are benches, and you can have a juice on the little terrace of a café. The view from here is wonderful: right opposite is St George’s Castle on its hill, and below are Alfama and the river. People from Lisbon love to come here in the evening, when the sky turns pink. You can sit here and even play tag.

lis-a-senhora-do-monte.s: One of the highest viewpoints in Lisbon is called Senhora do Monte. It is at the top of a hill reached by a steep street, so you have to climb it on foot. Next to it stands a little white chapel. From the viewpoint the city lies spread out before you: the castle, the bridges, the river and the hills that Lisbon stands on. They say this is the best place to watch the sunset, when the roofs turn orange. If you bring binoculars, you can make out the ships.

lis-a-bazilika-shtrela.s: In the Estrela area, a white dome gleams on a hill: this is the Estrela Basilica. It was built on the orders of Queen Maria the First at the end of the eighteenth century. The front is decorated with statues, and inside there is light marble of many colours. Nearby is a green garden with paths, a pond and a bandstand where music plays. And in the basilica there is also a huge nativity scene: about five hundred little figures made of cork and clay. You can look at them for a whole hour.

lis-a-sad-estufa-fria.s: In Eduardo VII Park, right in the centre of Lisbon, hides a garden called the Estufa Fria, the “Cold Greenhouse”. Long ago, stone was dug out of this place, and then plants were planted in the pit. Now it is cool, shady and green here: ferns, palms, bamboo, little ponds and waterfalls. Overhead is a wooden roof made of slats, and light comes through it. You walk along the paths, and the water babbles beside you. When it is hot, it is so pleasant here that you don’t want to leave.

lis-a-tramvaj-12.s: If the long tram number 28 wasn’t enough for you, take a ride on the little tram number 12. It goes in a circle: it starts at Figueira Square, climbs up the hills of Alfama and comes back to the same place. The little tram is short and yellow, with wooden seats. It passes the castle, the viewpoints and the narrow streets. The rails are so close to the houses that it feels as if you could touch the walls. The circle doesn’t take long, and you don’t have to change anywhere.

lis-a-funikuler-lavra.s: The Lavra funicular is the oldest in Lisbon. It began running in 1884 and is counted as a national monument. The car goes along a very steep street, and at the top a small garden with a view is waiting for it. It is quite short and yellow, with wooden seats inside. As with Lisbon’s other funiculars, one car goes up while the other comes down: they balance each other like the two ends of a seesaw. This machinery is still working today.

lis-a-kristu-rej.s: On the other bank of the Tagus, on a high cliff, stands the huge statue of Cristo Rei. It is a man with his arms stretched out to the sides, as if he were hugging the whole city. With its base, the statue is about a hundred and ten metres high, so you can see it from far away, even from Lisbon. It was built in 1959. Inside the base there is a lift that takes you up to a viewing platform. From there you can see the red bridge and the mouth of the river, where the Tagus flows into the ocean.

lis-a-kedr-printsipe-real.s: In the Príncipe Real garden, on a hill right in the centre of Lisbon, grows a huge old cedar. Its branches spread so wide that they are held up by posts, like a tent. Under the tree there is lots of shade, with benches and tables, and in summer children play there. Nearby on the square there is sometimes a fair, and under the garden itself a big underground water reservoir is hidden. Try walking round the tree in a circle and counting the posts.

lis-a-adamastor.s: At the Santa Catarina viewpoint, a stone giant sits among the rocks. This is Adamastor, a monster from an old poem about sailors. But here he doesn’t look scary: he is just a big, thoughtful head gazing into the distance. Street musicians play around him, and people sit on the steps and watch the sun set over the river. From here you can see the red bridge and the ships very well. And from the viewpoint, little streets run down to the waterfront.

us-ny-subway.s: The New York subway opened in 1904, more than a hundred years ago. Today it has over four hundred stations, and the trains run all day and all night, even in the middle of the night. At some stations, musicians sit playing guitars and violins. You are waiting for your train, and suddenly a little band is playing on the platform. Waiting is not boring at all.
a: Only when the sun is shining

us-ny-statenferry.s: In New York you can sail on the sea without paying a penny. The orange ferry goes from Manhattan to Staten Island, and the ride is free. It takes about twenty-five minutes. On the way, the ferry passes close to the Statue of Liberty, and the skyscrapers get smaller behind you. Seagulls fly along after the boat, the wind blows your hair about, and all the passengers, big and small, take photos of the city from the water.

us-dc-cherry.s: Every spring, thousands of cherry trees blossom in Washington, and the whole city turns pink and white. The trees came from Japan: in 1912 that country gave Washington about three thousand trees. The first two young trees were planted by the lake by the President’s wife and a lady visiting from Japan. Some of those very trees still flower today. With cherry blossom everywhere, it looks as if the city is covered in candyfloss.

us-sf-cablecar.s: Little wooden cars travel up and down the steep hills of San Francisco. They have no motor on the roof. Under the street, a long steel cable always runs along, and the car grabs it with a special grip and off it goes. The first cable car started in 1873. The driver pulls a lever, a bell rings, and the car climbs up a hill or rolls down it, while passengers stand on the steps.

us-sf-sealions.s: Sea lions live near Pier 39 in San Francisco. At the end of 1989, one came swimming in, then dozens more joined it, and by the start of the next year there were more than three hundred. They lie on wooden rafts by the boat harbour, push each other, bark loudly and are not the least bit afraid of people. The biggest ones are grown-up males, and they weigh up to four hundred kilograms.
a: On wooden rafts by the boat harbour
On the roof of a tram
On the benches in the park

us-fl-apollo.s: In Florida, at Cape Canaveral, there is a spaceport, and next to it is the Kennedy Space Center. On 16 July 1969, Apollo 11 took off from here with three astronauts. You could see their Saturn rocket from far away: it was almost a hundred and ten metres tall, like a house with more than thirty floors. Then people walked on the Moon for the very first time. The rocket’s launch could be heard for many kilometres around.
a: From a bridge in New York

us-fl-manatee.s: Off the coast of Florida swim gentle giants called manatees. People call them sea cows because they chew grass, only underwater grass: seaweed and sea grasses. A manatee is huge and weighs several hundred kilograms, but it is very calm. It swims slowly, and every few minutes it comes up to the surface to take a breath. In winter, when the water gets cold, manatees gather in warm springs and rivers to keep warm.

us-hi-kilauea.s: In Hawaii there is a volcano called Kilauea. Hawaiians say that the goddess of fire, Pele, lives in its crater. When the volcano wakes up, fountains of fire shoot out, and red-hot lava creeps down to the ocean. When it reaches the cold water, it hardens and breaks into tiny pieces. These pieces make black sand. On a beach like this, for example Punaluʻu, green sea turtles love to lie in the sun.

us-b-edison.s: Thomas Edison wanted to make a light bulb that would burn for a long time. Inside the glass bulb you need a very thin glowing thread. Edison and his helpers tried many different materials. In 1879, a burnt cotton thread glowed for more than thirteen hours. Then they tried bamboo, and that bulb burned for more than a thousand hours. So evenings became brighter, and homework by lamplight became easier.

us-b-popcorn.s: Why does a corn kernel jump in a hot pan and turn into a white fluffy cloud? Inside its hard shell it has a tiny drop of water. The heat turns the water into steam, the steam pushes from the inside, and suddenly the shell bursts: pop! Native Americans were eating popcorn many thousands of years ago. Today people love to eat it at the cinema. But not every kind of corn can pop. You need a special kind for popcorn.

old-first-hands.s: In caves all over the world, there are handprints that are many thousands of years old. One cave in Argentina is even called the Cave of the Hands. How were they made? A person pressed a hand to the rock and blew paint from their mouth through a tube made from a bone. The paint sprayed out, and under the hand a clean patch was left, the shape of a hand. Some of the hands are tiny, so little children took part in this art too!
a: They blew paint around the hand
They dipped the hand in honey
They drew it with a chocolate pencil

old-first-mammoth-house.s: In Ukraine, scientists dug up strange round houses. Their walls were built from mammoth bones and tusks! They were made about 18,000 years ago, when it was very cold, in the Ice Age. The bones were piled up like bricks, and animal skins were probably stretched over the top. Inside, people lit a fire, and it was warm. A house made of a mammoth, what an idea! But there were hardly any trees on the cold plains, and bones lay everywhere.

old-egypt-pyramid.s: The Great Pyramid at Giza was built as a tomb for the pharaoh Khufu. At first it was about 146 metres tall. It was made from around 2,300,000 blocks of stone! For more than 3,800 years it was the tallest building on Earth, and nobody could build higher. The record was only broken by a cathedral in England, finished in the Middle Ages. Just think: for 3,800 years, a pile of stones held the record!

old-egypt-cats.s: In Ancient Egypt, people loved cats very much. Cats caught mice in the barns, so the grain stayed safe. There was even a goddess with a cat’s head called Bastet. Egyptians often made cats out of clay and painted them on walls. When a pet cat died, the family was sad, and the Greek writer Herodotus said they even shaved off their eyebrows. Cats were wrapped up carefully, just like mummies. Lots of cat mummies have been found.
a: They caught mice and kept the grain safe
They could swim in the Nile on their backs

old-gr-olympia.s: The story says that the first Olympic Games were held in Greece about 2,800 years ago. They took place in a spot called Olympia, and not every year, but once every four years. Runners, wrestlers and discus throwers came from all the Greek cities. There were no gold medals back then! The winner got a crown of olive twigs on his head. For a Greek this was the greatest honour, and at home he was welcomed like a hero.
a: A gold medal on a ribbon

old-rm-teplyj-pol.s: Romans did not freeze in winter, not even in rich houses and baths. Their floors stood on low brick pillars, and under the floor a fire burned in a furnace. Hot air flowed through the empty space under the floor and through pipes in the walls. This system was called a hypocaust. So floor heating is not new: it was invented more than 2,000 years ago. But somebody had to look after the furnace by hand.

old-china-kites.s: Kites were invented in China more than two thousand years ago. Back then they were made from light silk and thin bamboo sticks, because paper came later. Kites were not only toys: they were part of festivals, and big kites were painted with dragons and birds. Today people fly kites on every continent. But the very first ones flew over Chinese fields, tied to a long silk string.

old-knights-armour.s: Many people think a knight in armour could hardly move. In fact, a full suit of armour weighed about twenty to twenty-five kilos, like a child at school. But it was made to fit the body, so the weight was spread out and did not sit on the shoulders. Armourers built it from lots of plates, so a knight could bend his arms and legs and even get on his horse by himself. The parts moved on rivets and little straps.
a: From one solid piece of stone

old-vik-longship.s: The Vikings sailed in long, narrow ships. Some had a carved dragon’s head at the front. The ship’s bottom was shallow, so it could go not only on the sea but also up small rivers. And if land blocked the way, the Vikings pulled the ship onto the shore and dragged it over logs to the next river. The boat was walking on land! There was one big sail, and when there was no wind, they took the oars.
a: They dragged the ship over the land on logs
They waited for the river to come to them
They took the ship apart and carried it in rucksacks

old-rus-onfim.s: About 750 years ago, a boy called Onfim lived in the city of Novgorod. He was six or seven and went to school. Onfim learned his letters and scratched them on pieces of birch bark. He drew too: a knight on a horse beating his enemy, and a scary beast. Under the beast he wrote: “I am a beast.” These bits of bark lay in the ground for almost seven centuries, until archaeologists found them. Now we can see how a boy from long ago loved to draw.
a: He learned letters and drew pictures

old-first-flute.s: More than 35,000 years ago, someone made a flute in a cave in Germany. It was carved from the wing bone of a big bird, a vulture, and it has five little holes for the fingers. The flute broke into pieces, but scientists found them and put them back together. It is about as long as a ruler, over twenty centimetres. So there was music when people still lived in caves and hunted mammoths.
a: From the bone of a big bird

old-egypt-tutankhamun.s: Pharaoh Tutankhamun became ruler when he was just a child, about nine years old. He lived around 3,300 years ago and did not rule for long. His tomb was found in 1922 by an Englishman, Howard Carter, and it was full of treasure: a golden mask, chariots, chairs, sandals. There were thousands of things! For a little boy, it was a whole room of toys and clothes that waited a very long time, until the scientists came.

old-gr-antikitera.s: In 1901, sponge divers found a sunken ship near the Greek island of Antikythera. Among the things was a lump of green bronze. Scientists found out that inside there were gears! It is a device more than 2,000 years old. It showed where the Sun and the Moon were in the sky, told people when an eclipse would come, and even counted the years until the next Olympic Games. A clock and a calendar in one box.
a: The Sun and the Moon moving, and eclipses
How many biscuits are left in the pantry

old-rm-priglashenie.s: Around the year 100, in the Roman fort of Vindolanda in the north of Britain, lived a woman called Claudia Severa. She wrote an invitation to her friend Sulpicia Lepidina for her birthday party. She wrote it in ink on a thin wooden tablet. At the end she added in her own hand: “I will wait for you, sister.” The tablet is still here today, so we can read the oldest party invitation.
a: On a card with a kitten
On a page from an exercise book

old-china-silk-thread.s: Silk is made by caterpillars called silkworms. They eat the leaves of the mulberry tree and then wrap themselves in a cocoon. The amazing part: the cocoon is made of just one single thread, hundreds of metres long! In ancient China, people learned to unwind the cocoons and weave the threads into soft, shiny cloth. The Chinese kept the secret of silk for many years, and the cloth travelled to far-away lands along the Silk Road.

old-knights-drawbridge.s: Around many castles people dug a deep ditch, called a moat, and sometimes filled it with water. A drawbridge led across the moat to the gate. In the daytime it was lowered, and carts and visitors came in. When danger came near, the guards pulled thick chains or ropes, and the bridge went up. It closed the gate like a big wooden door. It was hard to cross the moat without the bridge, so everyone in the castle felt safe.

old-vik-horns.s: You have probably seen pictures of a Viking in a helmet with big horns. But they never really had such helmets! Horns would get in the way in a cramped boat and catch on branches. A Viking helmet was plain and round, with a guard for the nose. Horned helmets were made up by artists and theatres about a hundred and fifty years ago, for fine costumes in the opera. A real Viking helmet was found in Norway. It is smooth, with no horns at all.
a: No, artists and theatres made up the horns
Yes, they scared cows with them
Yes, they carried water in the horns

old-rus-bortniki.s: In old Rus, as medieval Russia was called, honey came from wild bees. The honey hunters, called bortniki, found a thick tree with a hollow in the forest, or carved a hollow themselves. Bees moved in and made honey. The hollow could be very high up, ten metres above the ground. The bortnik climbed the tree, tied on with a rope, and took the honey carefully, so that the bees had enough for the winter. Honey was the main sweet treat, because there was no sugar then.

old-rm-termopolii.s: In the city of Pompeii there were fast-food shops on the streets, called thermopolia. They had a counter with round holes, and big pots of hot food were set into them. Not long ago, archaeologists dug up one of these shops almost whole. On the counter, ducks and a rooster are painted. Scientists think this was the menu: what is painted is what they sold. Bones left in the pots show that this is true.
a: Ducks and a rooster, like a menu

old-egypt-senet.s: The Egyptians loved to play. One of their favourite games was called senet: a board with three rows of ten squares, and playing pieces. Players took turns throwing sticks, like dice, and moved their pieces. Several senet boards were found in Tutankhamun’s tomb! But the rules were lost, and scientists still argue about how it was played. Today people play senet with made-up rules. Just think: the game is thousands of years old, and nobody knows the rules for sure!

por-lello.s: There is a bookshop in Porto called Lello. It is more than a hundred years old. In the middle of the shop, a red staircase rises up. It twists and splits in two, like a ribbon on a present. Above it shines a ceiling window of coloured glass, and the shelves are full of books right up to the top. It is one of the most beautiful bookshops in the world, and people from all over the Earth queue up to peek inside.

por-sao-bento.s: In Porto there is a train station called São Bento. When you walk into its big hall, it feels like you have stepped into a giant picture book. The walls are covered with white and blue tiles called azulejos, about twenty thousand of them! The tiles make pictures of olden times: kings and knights, and village parties. High up near the ceiling runs a colourful stripe. It shows how people travelled long ago, first in carts and later on the train.

por-clerigos.s: Above the roofs of Porto rises the Clérigos Tower, tall and thin like a pencil. An Italian architect, Nicolau Nasoni, designed it, and it was finished in 1763. At that time it was the tallest building in all of Portugal. To climb to the top, you must go up more than two hundred steps on a narrow spiral staircase. But from up there you can see the whole city: red roofs, the River Douro and boats on the water.

por-francesinha.s: In Porto people love a huge sandwich called the “francesinha”, which means “little French girl”. Inside there is bread, ham, sausage and a piece of meat. On top, it is covered with melted cheese and poured over with hot sauce, and often a fried egg sits on the very top like a little hat. You cannot pick this sandwich up with your hands. You eat it with a knife and fork. They say it was invented by a man who had lived in France for a long time and then came home to Porto.

por-a-thin-house.s: In Porto two churches, Carmo and Carmelitas, stand right next to each other. They say there was once a rule that two churches must not share a wall. So a tiny house was built between them, to keep the walls from touching. The house is so thin that you can hardly notice it: it is only about one metre wide. It has a white front and small windows, like a doll’s house. If you walk past, you may wonder how a person fits inside. But the house is real, and people really lived in it.
a: A thin house to live in
A tall tower with a clock

por-b-grape-harvest.s: In autumn, the grape harvest begins on the slopes of the Douro. The grapes are cut with scissors and carried in baskets. And then comes the funny part. The grapes are tipped into a low stone tank called a “lagar”, and people squash them with their bare feet, sometimes even to music! Some farms still do it this way today, although there are machines too. The juice comes out sweet and thick, and afterwards your feet stay purple for a long time.

por-b-iberian-wolf.s: In the mountains of northern Portugal lives the Iberian wolf. It is grey, with a dark stripe on its legs, and a little smaller than other wolves. Wolves live in families and carefully keep away from people. It is almost impossible to see them, but at night you can sometimes hear them calling to each other with howls. Wolves help keep the forest in order: they take the sick and weak animals.

por-ribeira.s: The old riverside of Porto is called Ribeira. The houses there are tall and narrow, and every one has a different colour: yellow, blue, pink, orange. They stand close together, shoulder to shoulder, like felt-tip pens in a box. Washing dries at the windows, and boats sail down on the River Douro. The old centre of Porto is so beautiful that the whole world looks after it like a treasure.

por-guimaraes.s: A cradle is a little bed for a baby. The city of Guimarães is called the cradle of Portugal, because this is where the country began. On an old city wall, big letters say: “Portugal was born here.” Above the town stands a stone castle with pointy towers. The first fort on this hill was built more than a thousand years ago.

por-braga.s: Near the city of Braga, a huge staircase leads up a high hill. It zigzags like a snake, and fountains splash on its landings. Next to it, a little funicular car goes up the hill, and since 1882 it has been moved by water! The top car is filled with water, so it gets heavier and rolls down, pulling the other car up on a cable. It is the oldest water-powered funicular in the world that still works.

por-a-douro-spain.s: The River Douro is not born in Portugal, but in the country next door, Spain. It is there too, but it is called the Duero. It flows for almost nine hundred kilometres, through fields, hills and vineyards. On the way its banks become steep, like steps for a giant. And in Porto the Douro finally reaches the ocean and flows into it. The river makes this long journey without a rest. What a tireless traveller!

por-a-tram-sea.s: Porto has tram line number one, and it is a special one. An old wooden tram leaves from the Ribeira and rolls along the River Douro. The wheels clatter softly, the seats are made of wood, and the windows are open. The further you go, the wider the river gets, until the ocean appears. The last stop is in the Foz area, where the Douro meets the sea. Passengers get off and go for a walk along the shore, to breathe the salty wind and watch the waves.
a: To the ocean, along the river
To the mountains in the north

por-a-dragon-stadium.s: The football club Porto has blue and white colours, and a dragon sits on its badge. The team’s stadium is called the “Estádio do Dragão”, which means “Dragon Stadium”. It opened in 2003 and holds about fifty thousand people. When the team plays, the stands sing songs and wave flags and scarves. On the pitch a cheerful mascot runs around. It is a dragon too, and its name is Draco. You can spot the fans in the city at once by their blue and white scarves.

por-a-henry-born.s: More than six hundred years ago, a boy called Henry was born in Porto, so people believe. He was a prince, but he liked maps and ships more than feasts. When he grew up, he gathered sailors, builders and scientists to look for new sea routes. That is why he was later nicknamed the Navigator. He hardly went on long voyages himself, but he thought up ways for ships to sail further. In Porto there is still an old house where, so the story goes, he was born.

por-a-bolhao.s: In the centre of Porto stands the old Bolhão market. In the past you could buy everything in its aisles: vegetables, fruit, fish, flowers, cheese and fresh bread. The sellers called out loudly to shoppers and told jokes. Above the rows there are tall balconies with iron railings, and below it smells of greens and the sea. The market was repaired for several years and opened again in 2022. Now it is noisy again, and very tasty. Children love to look at the bright heaps of apples and oranges.

por-b-caldo-verde.s: In the north of Portugal people love “caldo verde”, which means green soup. It is made of potatoes and a special cabbage with big leaves, cut into very, very thin strips. A spoonful of olive oil goes into the bowl, and sometimes a slice of sausage. The soup is warm, thick and tasty. People serve it at parties, and at home when it is cold and drizzling outside.

por-a-crystal-peacocks.s: Porto has a big garden around the former Crystal Palace. The palace of glass and iron was once built for an exhibition, and later it was gone, but the garden stayed. Peacocks walk calmly along the paths. They spread their huge tails like green and blue fans and call out proudly. Tall trees and flowers grow nearby, and from the edge of the garden you can see the River Douro. Children love to come here to watch the birds and play on the grass. But you must not touch the peacocks!

por-douro.s: In the valley of the River Douro, the steep mountain sides are turned into huge steps. They are called terraces. For many years, people built each step from stones with their own hands. Grapes grow on the terraces, and in autumn they are picked into baskets. The steps stretch far, far along the river, and it looks as if a giant built himself a staircase up to the sky.

por-viana.s: The north of Portugal is famous for filigree jewellery. Craftspeople twist golden threads, thin as a hair, and lay them out in patterns like lace. The most famous piece is the Heart of Viana, named after the town of Viana do Castelo. On holidays, the girls there put on bright embroidered dresses, mostly red ones, and lots of gold jewellery. When they walk down the street, everything around them sparkles.

por-geres.s: In the north of Portugal there is the country’s only national park, Peneda-Gerês. It has high mountains, waterfalls and thick forests. Little Garrano ponies roam free on the slopes. They are small and brown, with a thick mane and fringe. They are very strong and walk nimbly over the rocks. Eagles, roe deer and even wolves live in this park too.

por-a-luis-two-floors.s: Over the River Douro in Porto hangs a big iron bridge called Dom Luís. It has two floors! Down below, almost at the water, cars drive and people walk. Up above, very high, people stroll and little metro trains run. The bridge rests on a huge iron arch, and the arch looks like a rainbow made of metal. If you stand on the top floor, you can see the whole city: red roofs, boats and coloured houses. The top floor opened a very long time ago, in 1886, and the lower one a year later. The bridge still works today.

por-a-maria-pia.s: Next to the big Luís bridge stands another one. It is smaller and very thin, like lace made of iron. It was named after Queen Maria Pia. It was built by the company of Gustave Eiffel, a Frenchman, the very one whose tower stands in Paris. Trains crossed the bridge for many years, and you could see them from far away. Now there are no trains there, because a new bridge was built next to it. But the lovely old bridge still stands over the Douro, making everyone happy who sails along the river.

por-a-six-bridges.s: In Porto there is a fun river trip called “Six Bridges”. A little boat sails along the Douro, and the bridges pass over your head one after another. Here is the lovely old Maria Pia, here is the two-floor Dom Luís, here is the Arrábida bridge with one huge concrete arch. All the bridges are different: each has its own shape and its own age. The children on the deck wave to the people on the bridges, and they wave back. Try to count the bridges together with the guide!

por-a-rabelo.s: By the quay in Porto stand old rabelo boats. They have flat bottoms, one square sail, and a rudder as long as a giant’s oar. In the old days, boats like these carried heavy barrels of wine along the Douro, from the vineyards to the city. The river is fast there, with rocks and bends, so the boatmen had to be very skilful. Today the rabelos no longer carry barrels every day, but they are prettily decorated, and each one has the name of a wine house painted on it. Tourists and children love to look at them.

por-a-gaia-cellars.s: Across from Porto, on the other bank of the Douro, lies the town of Vila Nova de Gaia. There are many old cellars there where port wine is left to age. In a cellar it is always dark and cool, and the air smells of wood. Huge barrels lie in rows, and the wine sleeps in them for years, and sometimes for decades. The workers walk between the barrels and check how the wine is feeling. Above the cellar roofs you can see big signs, and from there you can see the whole of Porto.

por-a-barrel-secret.s: Port wine is made from grapes that grow on the slopes of the Douro valley. It has a secret. When the grape juice starts to ferment, a strong drink made from grapes is added to it. Then the fermenting stops, but the sweetness stays. That is why port wine is sweet and thick. After that, it is poured into big wooden barrels called “pipas”. One such barrel holds about five hundred and fifty litres. Children are not given port wine, but of course they love to taste the grapes from those slopes!

por-a-sandeman-don.s: Above the quay in Gaia hangs a big black figure. It is a man in a long cloak, like the students of Porto wear, and a hat with a wide brim. His name is simply Don. He is the sign of one wine house, Sandeman, and he was drawn as long ago as about 1928. He is so famous that even people who have never been to Porto know him. Don stands very still, like a hero from a fairy tale, and seems to guard the cellars. Children like to spot him from far away and take photos of him with the river behind.
a: A black cloak and a hat
A red jacket and a cap
A white coat and a tall hat

por-a-lello-motto.s: The Lello bookshop in Porto looks like a hall from a fairy tale. There is wood, carved columns, a staircase, and above your head a ceiling of coloured glass. A motto is written on it in Latin: “Decus in labore”. It means “Honour in work”. The Lello brothers, who opened the shop in 1906, chose it. They wanted work to be honoured and books to be beautiful. Step inside and look up: the light from the glass falls right onto the spines, and the books seem to glow.
a: On the cover of every book

por-a-lello-rails.s: The Lello bookshop has a secret under your feet. Little rails run across the floor, like for a toy train! They say that, in the old days, trolleys of books were rolled along them from the entrance to the staircase. That made it easier for the workers to carry heavy piles. Now you hardly ever see trolleys, but the rails have stayed as a memory. They remind us that the shop is very old and that books were really cared for here. Look at the floor when you are there, and find the thin tracks.

por-a-tram-museum.s: Porto has a whole tram museum. It is in a former power station by the river, in the Massarelos district. Inside stand old trams, and the wood and the brass handles gleam. In the old days, back in 1872, horses and mules pulled the trams along the city’s rails, and then electricity arrived. In the museum you can touch the benches and imagine how people rode to work many years ago. And next to the museum, old trams still run today!

por-a-boavista-chess.s: Porto has another famous football team, called Boavista. Its players run onto the pitch in an unusual kit: black and white squares, like a chessboard! The Portuguese even call it the “chess” team. Its stadium is called the Bessa, and it is not at all as huge as the Dragon’s, but it is very cosy. Boavista fans wear checks too, and you can spot them from far away. So, in one city, two very different teams live side by side.

por-a-tile-houses.s: In Porto, many houses are dressed in tiles, like a bright shirt. These tiles are called azulejos. They are not only pretty, but also very useful. It often rains here, and a damp wind blows in from the ocean. The tiles keep the water out of the walls, and the house stays dry and warm. Some houses are covered in white tiles, others in blue, and others in patterns. If you walk along the streets, it is like a whole exhibition of pictures on the walls.
a: To keep the damp out of the walls

por-a-carmo-wall.s: One of the churches in Porto, Carmo, has a huge picture made of blue tiles on its side. It appeared in the early 1900s. The tiles show saints and scenes from the lives of the Carmelite monks, and golden frames shine all around. The picture covers the whole tall side wall, so people walking by often stop and look up. Rain and sun do not harm it: the tiles hardly change. It is so bright that it seems the sky has come down onto the wall.

por-a-bolsa-arab.s: In Porto there is the Stock Exchange Palace, where merchants once worked. The most beautiful place in it is the Arab Room. Its walls and ceiling are covered in fine patterns and gold, and the light from the chandeliers glitters on every curl. The room took very many years to build, and the craftsmen carved every pattern by hand. In the past, important guests were welcomed here, and today tourists come on tours. When children walk in, they usually freeze and whisper, “It’s like a fairy tale!”

por-a-casa-musica.s: In Porto stands an extraordinary building. It is called Casa da Música, which means House of Music. The building is white and angular, like a huge precious stone or a lump of ice. It opened in 2005, and it was designed by an architect from the Netherlands. Inside there are big halls where orchestras, pianists and drummers play. Sometimes there are concerts for children, and the sound there is so clear that you can hear every note. And on the square in front of the building, people love to ride scooters and skateboards.

por-a-tripeiros.s: The people of Porto, in Portugal, are playfully called “tripeiros”. The word sounds funny, but it is not unkind. The story goes that, long, long ago, the townspeople gave all the best meat to the ships that were sailing off on long voyages. They kept only what was left, and learned to cook very tasty dishes from it. One of those dishes became famous, and the town still loves it today. And the people of Porto wear their nickname proudly, like a merry secret.

por-a-matosinhos-sardines.s: Not far from Porto, right by the ocean, lies the fishing town of Matosinhos. Here the fishermen bring fresh fish straight from their boats. People especially love sardines. They are grilled over coals right in the street, and the smoke smells all over the neighbourhood. The sardine is served on a slice of bread, with baked potatoes and peppers. You have to eat it with your hands, and nobody minds if your fingers get salty. Children try it too, although at first they are a little afraid of the bones.

por-a-foz-ocean.s: At the very end of its journey, the River Douro reaches the ocean. This place is called Foz do Douro. Here the river is already wide and calm, and the ocean is noisy and strong. Waves crash against the stone pier, spray flies up, and seagulls cry overhead. On the shore stand an old lighthouse and a handsome fort. You can sit on the promenade and watch fresh water mix with salty water. And in the evening, the sun sets right into the ocean, and everything around turns pink.

por-a-laundry-ribeira.s: In the old Ribeira district of Porto, the streets are narrow and the houses stand close together. Washing dries on lines from the windows: shirts, dresses, towels, little socks. The wind sways it all, and it looks as if the streets are decorated with flags. It is not a holiday, just an ordinary day. People in Porto are used to drying things in the sun and wind, as their grandmothers did. Tourists are usually surprised, and then they take photos. If you look from below, it makes the merriest garland ever!

por-a-majestic-cafe.s: On Santa Catarina Street in Porto there is the Majestic café, which opened in 1921. Inside are big mirrors, carved wood, soft armchairs and plaster decorations under the ceiling. Waiters in white shirts and black waistcoats walk around without any hurry. In the old days, poets, painters and ordinary townspeople came here to talk over a cup of coffee. The café looks like a palace. Children drink hot chocolate there and look at the golden curls. And there is often a queue at the door, because everyone wants to go in.

por-a-se-cathedral.s: High above the river, right on the hill, stands the cathedral of Porto, called the Sé. It is grey, thick and strong, with two towers, like a little fortress. It was built a very long time ago, about nine hundred years ago. Inside it is cool and quiet, and next to it there is a long gallery around a courtyard. Its walls are decorated with blue tile pictures. From the square in front of the cathedral you can see the Douro, the bridges and the red roofs of the city. Many people come here to watch the sunset.

por-a-serralves-pink.s: On the edge of Porto stands a pink house, and it looks like a castle made of cake. It is called Serralves, and it was built almost a hundred years ago. The house has straight lines and pretty windows. This style is called Art Deco. All around is a huge park with tall trees, a pond and green lawns. Families stroll along the paths, children run about, and birds sing in the treetops. Today, in the house and in the museum next to it, they show modern art. It is great for a picnic in good weather.

por-b-douro-terraces.s: The banks of the River Douro are so steep that there is hardly any flat land there. But grapes love sun and warm slopes. So people had an idea: terraces. They built low walls from stone and filled them with earth. The result was huge green steps that climb from the water right up to the sky. In autumn the leaves turn yellow and red, and the slopes become golden. UNESCO protects this beauty.

por-b-rabelo-boat.s: In the old days, barrels of wine were carried along the River Douro on special boats called rabelos. A rabelo has a wide flat bottom, so it is not afraid of shallow places, and one big sail. It is steered not with a rudder but with a very, very long oar at the back. The steersman stands high up and skilfully guides the boat between the rocks. Today barrels are carried in other ways, and the rabelos stand by the quay in Porto and take tourists for rides.
a: With a long oar at the back
With a rope from the bank

por-b-green-wine.s: In the north of Portugal, in the Minho region, they make “green wine”, called vinho verde. It is not green at all: it is white, rosé or red. Here, “green” means “young”. It is drunk right away, while it is fresh and tickles a tiny bit with bubbles. It is a drink for grown-ups, and children drink juice. But the grapes themselves grow thickly in these parts, all over the green land.

por-b-vines-on-trees.s: It rains a lot in Minho, and the ground there is damp. If the vine creeps low, the berries spoil. So, in the old days, people planted the vine by trees and let it grow up the trunks. The vine climbed onto the branches, and the bunches hung high up, in the wind and the sun. In some places this kind of grape still grows today: it winds around posts and poles along roads and fields.

por-b-rainy-minho.s: Minho is one of the rainiest regions of Portugal. Warm, damp air comes in from the ocean, the clouds catch on the mountains and pour down as rain. That is why everything here is so green: the meadows, the forests, the mossy stone walls. The rivers are full of water, and little streams run down the slopes. If you travel to the north, take an umbrella with you, but don’t be sad: after the rain it smells of grass and wet earth.

por-b-douro-lock.s: There are dams on the River Douro, so ships cannot simply sail past. Locks were built for them, like big water lifts. The ship sails into a stone chamber, the gates close, and the water quietly lifts it up or lowers it down. The lock at Carrapatelo is one of the deepest in Europe: the ship changes height by about thirty-five metres, like in a house with ten floors.
a: They go through a lock, like a lift

por-b-pinhao-station.s: A railway runs along the River Douro, and the train runs beside the water all the time. At the station in Pinhão, the walls are covered with blue tiles, azulejos. They show vineyards: how people work on the slopes, pick bunches of grapes and carry them in boats. While you wait for the train, you can look at the tiles like a picture book. And then look out of the window at the real hills.
a: Vineyards and work on the slopes

por-b-roman-braga.s: Braga is one of the oldest cities in Portugal. It was founded by the Romans, who called it Bracara Augusta, after the Emperor Augustus. Back then there were roads, temples and stone houses here. Now, where the Roman town stood, there are churches, squares and cafés. And in the middle rises an old cathedral, said to be one of the oldest in the country. You walk down the street, and you are stepping on ground that is more than two thousand years old.

por-b-bom-jesus.s: In the old centre of Braga there is an unusual spring. It was carved right into a big granite rock. On the stone there is a little figure of a man in long clothes, and next to it are letters in Latin. They say these are dedicated to the local water gods. The spring is about two thousand years old, and now a bright building has been put up over it, so that rain and wind do not wear the carving away. You can look inside and see the ancient stone very close.

por-b-guimaraes-palace.s: In Guimarães there is an old palace of the dukes. It was begun long ago, in the fifteenth century, from stone and brick. From far away, it looks like a fairy-tale castle: tall brick chimneys stick up on the roof, and it seems that every room has a fire burning. Inside there are big halls and old carpets on the walls. And next to it stands a castle on a rock, even older.

por-b-penha-cablecar.s: A cable car goes from Guimarães up the Penha mountain. The cabin glides over the trees, and the town below becomes very small. At the top there is a forest, paths and huge round boulders, lying as if a giant had scattered pebbles. You can climb up on a rock and look around. It is lovely to walk there: it smells of pine needles, and birds sing in the branches.

por-b-briteiros.s: Not far from Guimarães, on a hill, lies the ancient village of Briteiros. About two thousand years ago, people lived here whom we usually call the Celts. Their houses were round, made of stone, and the roofs were most likely thatched. Now there are no roofs, but the stone rings of the walls have survived, and you can walk among them. You can see streets and steps, and it seems that the people have only just stepped out.
